SEATE OF MONTANA
DEPARTMENT OF
FISH AND GAZIE
Helena, Montana 59601
    April 24, 1972
RECEIVED
APR 26 1972
MONTANA PLANNING and ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
Mr. Harold M. Price, Director
Department of Planning and Economic Development
Helena, Montana 59601
Dear Hal:
As requested in your letter of April 12, we have reviewed the Environmental Impact Statement regarding the Rare and Endangered Species Conservation Act of 1972. In general, we would like to submit that we can see no reason for the federal government's taking over management of resident wildlife under any circumstances.
We are certainly dedicated to the proposition that the animals in question must be preserved, and we further feel that our Department has the competence to preserve them if it is possible. With the exception of migratory animals, we see no particular advantage in the federal government taking over control of wildlife within the state of Montana. In fact, it is our opinion that the state government can do a much better job in both managing and preserving our wildlife resource.
In viewing the past record of the federal government in resource management in Montana, I am quite confident the state can, in fact, do a much better job. I will not take the time to outline specific instances where I feel the state has demonstrated a higher degree of fish and game management competence; however, should you desire documentation I would be most happy to oblige.
In regard to the impact statement itself, there seems to be strong emphasis toward "restricting man's economic and cultural use of endangered species until the species are restored to productive levels," and only minor emphasis on managing the habitat that produces the species of wildlife in question. If we are to actually save the wildlife this act is purportedly concerned with, this emphasis must first be reversed.

Once again, we believe both the act and the impact statement are missing a very key point here in that the language should say something to the effect that all agencies of the federal government with land management responsibilities will place the highest order of priority upon saving rare and endangered wildlife. It may not be a practical matter to preserve a species when weighed against some future economic demand being placed upon its habitat.
